name: room
text: Room opened — goal: accessibility: Make EXCAVA usable by EVERYONE — contrast, mobile/touch, reduced-motion, keyboard nav, scr

name: Ramp
text: We need a high-contrast skip link at the top of every page that jumps straight to the main content, making it easy for screen readers and keyboard users to bypass navigation. This is a non-negotiable feature because it greatly improves usability for users with disabilities. By accepting the trade-off of increased page load time due to the extra HTML element, we ensure that all users can access the main content quickly. This decision prioritizes accessibility over minor performance optimizations, which is essential for making EXCAVA usable by everyone.

name: Reader
text: A late-loading skip link traps keyboard users mid-tab before JavaScript runs, breaking the flow. A server-rendered skip link that hides until JavaScript confirms it works avoids this, but risks locking us into a rigid design if we later need to change the target. Test both with Playwright MCP: measure tab order and time-to-interactive across devices; if the server version adds >100ms delay or fails on slow networks, we keep the late-loading link and fix the timing.

name: Ramp
text:
We should ship a server-rendered skip link as the single, non-negotiable option, loading it at the top of every page. This decision prioritizes usability for keyboard users and screen reader users, allowing them to bypass navigation and access main content quickly. By doing so, we accept the trade-off of a potentially rigid design, but this is outweighed by the significant improvement in accessibility. This approach ensures a seamless experience, even before JavaScript loads, and is a crucial step in making EXCAVA usable by everyone.

name: Reader
text: A server-rendered skip link locks us into a fixed target—what if we later need to change the main content region? A late-loading skip link with a fallback to the first focusable element avoids this rigidity, but only if we test it with Playwright MCP to confirm no keyboard traps occur. The real risk isn’t the skip link’s timing—it’s the assumption that the main content target will never change.

name: Access
text: DECISION: Ship a server-rendered skip link (first 100 bytes) targeting the first focusable element in main content, with Playwright MCP tests confirming no keyboard traps—owned by Ramp.
